name: Warren Buffett
role: Investor, chairman and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway; philanthropist
summary: Buffett is a businessman who speaks publicly on economic policy more than on social or foreign questions. He praises the market system while favouring higher taxes on the very rich, an estate tax, an expanded Earned Income Tax Credit and safety nets, and opposes a large minimum-wage increase. He argues for balanced trade over persistent deficits and has called climate risk worth acting on early.

sources.usedFor: Summary of his stated views on health-care costs, estate tax, taxes, population growth

universal-healthcare.rationale: Reported as supporting the aim of expanding health insurance coverage while calling the 2010 reform insufficient on costs; no stated position on state-provided universal care.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In his 2015 Wall Street Journal op-ed he wrote that a $15 minimum 'would almost certainly reduce employment in a major way'; he preferred an expanded EITC and called smaller increases welcome but insufficient.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: 2015 letter: 'Nothing rivals the market system in producing what people want'; he also endorses safety nets and regulated utilities, so not an absolute view.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In his 2011 New York Times op-ed he urged Congress to raise rates on very high incomes, saying he paid 17.4% of taxable income against 33-41% for his office staff and that higher taxes would not deter investment. His 2003 letter also records his criticism of the Bush tax proposals.

cut-welfare.rationale: His 2015 letter calls for 'a variety of safety nets' for people whose skills the market values little and says prosperity should not mean penury for the unfortunate; he did not address dependency arguments.

state-harmful.rationale: He calls for government action and approves government rescue in 2008 and regulated utilities; no direct statement on the state's necessity.

reduce-immigration.rationale: No stated position on immigration levels; praising immigrants in the 2016 letter is something nearby.

free-trade.rationale: 2004 letter: 'true trade' is 'enormously beneficial for both us and them... the more of this, the better', agreeing with Adam Smith. He objects to persistent one-way deficits and in 2025 said balanced trade is good, so his support is qualified.

tax-inheritance.rationale: He testified to the Senate that a meaningful estate tax is needed and opposed repeal; he did not say how heavy it should be.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: In 2025 he said trade should not be a weapon and that import certificates, his own balance-of-trade scheme, were better than current tariff policy. His 2003 import-certificate plan is not a tariff but he described it as gimmicky; overall he opposes tariffs.

limit-population.rationale: Reported to have expressed concern about unchecked population growth and long supported family planning; no policy statement found.

taxation-theft.rationale: He repeatedly argues the rich should pay more tax and says Berkshire expects and ought to pay much more; this is incompatible with calling taxation theft, though he never addressed the claim directly.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He advocates safety nets, an expanded EITC, estate tax and higher taxes on the rich, which goes beyond a limited state; he did not address the doctrine by name.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: 2001 letter: Berkshire never considers religion, gender, race or sexual orientation in hiring or purchasing, and it 'would not only be wrong to do so, it would be idiotic'. He did not address legal rights.

trade-surplus.rationale: 2004 letter: a $0.6 trillion US surplus would be 'mercantilism – a long-discredited economic strategy' that he 'would condemn'; he sought balanced trade rather than surpluses.

precautionary-principle.rationale: 2015 letter: it would be foolish to demand 100% proof of climate damage if prompt action had even a small chance of thwarting it ('Noah's Law'). He framed it for individuals and insurers, not as a statement on regulation specifically.

flat-income-tax.rationale: His proposal was for higher rates at the top (above $1 million, more above $10 million), which is the opposite of a flat rate; he did not address the flat tax by name.

no-bailouts.rationale: 2008 letter: 'strong and immediate action by government was essential' to avoid a total breakdown of the financial system, while warning of inflation and dependence on aid.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: He states that trade is enormously beneficial and the more the better, which contradicts a bloc shut off from outside trade.

corporate-influence.rationale: 2004 letter describes 'check-waving CEOs' who 'muscled Congress' over option accounting and urges shareholders to contact legislators.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: He credits the market system with delivering 'abundance beyond any dreams of our forefathers' (2016 letter) while noting its losers.

social-market-economy.rationale: He pairs strong praise of the market system with safety nets and an expanded EITC, and approves fair regulation of utilities.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He said a meaningful estate tax is needed 'to prevent our democracy from becoming a dynastic plutocracy' and called dynastic wealth contrary to what built the country.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: He personally favours a 'reformed and expanded Earned Income Tax Credit' (2015 letter) and argued in his WSJ op-ed that it rewards work without distorting markets.

notes: Positions come mostly from shareholder letters and press accounts of op-eds; the original New York Times (2011, 2012), Fortune (2003) and Wall Street Journal (2015) texts could not be opened, so those are cited through quoting articles. He rarely speaks on social issues; his foundation's giving and his political endorsements are not treated as positions.
